segments.english: §14. See and understand, our friend the pleasant reader, how our honored Rabbi Tam, the aforementioned, cried out like a herald against those who engage in the new Kabbalah, for they breached the fences of the Torah, and laid bare, laid bare, its foundations and its roots in the unity of the Name, may He be blessed, as will be explained below. Instead of thinking to draw near to the Name, may He be blessed, they strayed from the way and came to believe in many other gods, and to worship them! And like the words of Rabbi Tam ben Yachya, Mahari Albo also wrote in the Ikkarim, chapter 28, of the second. And further he expounded at length in the book Ravid ha-Zahav, and also brought the words of the great Rabbi Maharshal, in his responsa and in the work Yam shel Shlomo, against those who boast of the novelties they study in Kabbalah. And he wrote that since the Talmud was sealed, we may not be stringent against the Gemara, and it is like heresy, as explained at length in Chok Ya'akov, section 489, subsection 11. All this is according to the assumption and the ascription whereby they ascribed the Zohar to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the Tanna, but after the criticism which the wise of heart examined and investigated after him, from whose womb the things mentioned in it came out, and when the work mentioned came out, and from whose hand it came out, it was explained very plainly that it is a work of one of the latter ones, and those ideas did not come out of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the Tanna, peace be upon him, at all, for in it are found many things in the fundamentals of the faith of our holy Torah contrary to the words of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai in the Talmud and in the Midrashim of our Rabbis of blessed memory, famous in Israel, certainly one must not rely on it in any matter touching the customs of Israel that our forebears practised. And the sages of the Middle Ages did not do well, who changed upon us several things in the prayer books, according to the Zohar and the Kabbalists, for some of those changes lead to heresy, to believe in many powers and to worship other gods, as will be explained below.

tokens.note: The printed word is נעלם ("hidden"); the context and the author's address elsewhere ("קורא נעים", "pleasant reader") point to נעים. Translated as "pleasant"; see apparatus.
כמה"ר: כבוד מורנו הרב רבי, "the honored Morenu ha-Rav Rabbi", an honorific; the author gives it to Rabbi Tam.
ככרוכיא: a herald or town crier (karukya).
וערו ערו: a doubled verb; the English keeps it doubled.

tokens.gloss: the Name, may He be blessed
tokens.note: השי"ת: the Name, may He be blessed (fixed form).

tokens.gloss: to the Name, may He be blessed

tokens.note: והאמין: the Hebrew has the singular verb after the plural ובאו; translated as plural ("came to believe").
כ': כתב, "wrote" (the author's abbreviation for the verb, as in 3:14.81 וכתב).
מהר"י אלבו: Morenu ha-Rav Rabbi Y. Albo, the author of the Ikkarim; the text names him only by the acronym.
משני: the second treatise of the Ikkarim.
מהרש"ל: the acronym of morenu ha-Rav Rabbi Shlomo Luria; the text gives only the acronym and the title of his book.
אין לנו להחמיר: "it is not for us to be stringent", i.e. we may not; it is the ground for "like heresy".
תפ"ט: the letters tav, pe, tet, which make 489.
י"א: the subsection number, 11.
חכמי לב: "the wise of heart", Exod 28:3 (also 31:6).
מבטן מי יצאו: echoes Job 38:29 "מבטן מי יצא הקרח" ("from whose womb did the ice come forth"); the author uses the question form for the origin of the Zohar.
The Hebrew full stop after יצא ends a clause with no main clause: the main clause is ונתבאר in the next sentence. The English joins them with a comma.
באר היטב: Deut 27:8 "באר היטב" ("very plainly"); the English reads the two words as one adverb phrase.
חיבור אחד האחרונים: construct, "a work of one of the latter ones" (the Aharonim, the later authorities), not "a single work".
ע"ה: peace be upon him.
ימי הבינים: the Middle Ages, the author's period term.

grammar: ראה והבן ... איך ... צוח: 'see and understand how ... cried out'; the two imperatives open one long period, which runs to the end of the paragraph.
ותחת אשר חשבו להתקרב ... תעו: 'instead of thinking to draw near, they strayed'; the author sets the intention against the act.
וכדברי ר' תם ... כ' גם כן מהר"י אלבו: כ' is כתב; the verb comes first in the Hebrew and the English places it after the name.

וכתב דמאחר ... אין לנו להחמיר ... והוי כמו מינות: an indirect report with no quotation marks; אין לנו + infinitive is 'it is not for us to ...' (we may not), so the stringency against the Gemara is itself 'like heresy'.
וכל זה הוא לפי ההנחה והיחוס: 'all this is according to the assumption and the ascription'; the ascription to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is what is disputed.

אך אחרי הבקורת ... ומיד מי יצא. ונתבאר ... כי הוא חיבור אחד האחרונים: the long clause after אחרי has no main clause of its own; the main clause is ונתבאר. The English joins them with a comma. חיבור אחד האחרונים is a construct, 'a work of one of the latter ones'.
segments.note: The paragraph is a single period with a report of two authorities at its end. The Wikisource base text is used; the 1931 scan is not collated.
apparatus: Allusion, not quotation: 'אלהים אחרים' echoes Exod 20:3 ('other gods'); the English follows the author's wording.
Printed 'קורא נעלם' (3:14.5-6), 'hidden reader': translated 'pleasant reader' (the author's 'קורא נעים'); the printed word is likely a misprint for נעים.
Ps 137:7 'ערו ערו עד היסוד בה' ('Strip it, strip it, down to its foundation'): echoed in 'וערו ערו יסודותיה' (3:14.22-24); the English keeps 'laid bare, laid bare'.
Job 38:29: 'מבטן מי יצא' ('from whose womb did ... come forth') in 'מבטן מי יצאו הדברים' (3:14.119-121).
Base text is Wikisource; a general line until the 1931 scan is collated (open question 2).

segments.english: §15. Also the Rav Ravid ha-Zahav brought further the words of Maran in Beit Yosef, who was concerned about the words of the Zohar in a place where the Gemara does not mention anything contrary to its words. And the Rema, of blessed memory, wrote about him that although the Gemara does not mention anything contrary to its words, there is no basis for this in the words of the decisors, and one need not be concerned with the words of the Zohar, see there. Further he brought the words of the Radbaz, of blessed memory, that he wrote that every matter mentioned in the Gemara or in one of the decisors or the masters of the halakhot, even if it be contrary to what is written in the books of Kabbalah, I rule on it, both to be lenient and to be strict, and I will not be concerned with what is written in those books. As for myself, if it is a stringency, I follow it and if a leniency, I will not be concerned with it. Further he wrote in the name of the Ra'em and other decisors that one need not be concerned about the words of the Kabbalists against any decisor, see there. Say now, that from the words of the decisors mentioned in the responsum of the Rav Ravid ha-Zahav, and they are Maran, of blessed memory, and Moreinu ha-Rav Moshe, and the Radbaz, and the Kenesset ha-Gedolah, and Mahari ha-Levi, K., Maharash ha-Levi and Rabbi Eliyahu ha-Levi, and Rabbi Moshe Alkaboli, and Rabbi Tam ben Yachya, and the Rav Chok Ya'akov, and Maharshal, and Maharam al-Shakar, who say that one need not be concerned with the words of the Zohar and the Kabbalists, when they are against the Mishnah and the Talmud, and even against a single decisor. Behold, from this prove to yourself that you wrote that they are a law of Moses from Sinai, that your words are a fabrication and utter folly.

tokens.note: הר': ha-Rav, before the title of a book (no בעל or מחבר): "the Rav Ravid ha-Zahav". The text names no one.
מרן: the author's honorific for the writer of the Beit Yosef; the text names no one. Literally 'our master'.
בב"י: Beit Yosef, the commentary on the Tur.
הרמ"א: the Rema, Rabbi Moshe Isserles.
אין לזה מדברי הפוסקים: elliptical, "there is nothing for this from the words of the decisors"; "basis" is supplied by the English to complete it.
ע"ש: עיין שם, "see there".
הרדב"ז: the Radbaz, Rabbi David ibn Zimra.
הרא"ם: the Ra'em.
ע"ש: עיין שם, "see there".
The Hebrew prints רבי ("Rabbi"); the likelier word is רביד, as at 3:15.6. Translated by the context; see apparatus.
הזהב: the Hebrew prints "הרב רבי הזהב"; read as "the Rav Ravid ha-Zahav" (see 3:15.109 and apparatus).
ומור"ם: ומורנו הרב משה, "and Moreinu ha-Rav Moshe"; the text gives only this form.
כנה"ג: the Kenesset ha-Gedolah.
כ': an abbreviation inside a list of names; "wrote" (כתב) leaves the verb without an object, and כבוד ("the honored") or כן ("likewise") are also possible. Left as the initial "K." (see apparatus).
הר"מ: read as Rabbi Moshe; the abbreviation is not expanded in the text.
The Hebrew prints אלקבולי; possibly a form of Alkabetz (אלקבץ), but the printed spelling is kept.
מהר"ם אלשקר: Maharam al-Shakar, as the author writes him.
שהוא: the Hebrew has the singular "that it is"; the English reads it of the words of the Zohar and the Kabbalists together ("when they are").
הוכיח: the printed form is the perfect "he proved"; read as the imperative הוכח, "prove", after אמור in the same passage.

grammar: גם הביא עוד ... וכתב עליו ... שכתב שכל דבר: the reporting verbs carry indirect speech throughout the paragraph, so the English has no quotation marks.
שכתב שכל דבר ... אני מורה בו ... ולעצמי: the Radbaz's words are reported in indirect speech, and the first person ('I rule', 'I follow') is kept.
הנה מזה הוכיח לעצמך: the closing turn is addressed to a second person, whom the author charges with calling these rulings 'a law of Moses from Sinai'.

אמור מעתה שמדברי הפוסקים ... והם ... שאומרים ... הנה מזה: the sentence breaks off after the list of decisors and the closing turn begins at הנה; the words 'the words of' (מדברי) are kept in the English.
segments.note: The paragraph reports a sequence of decisors and ends with the author's address to his opponent. The base text is Wikisource.
apparatus: The printed 'הרב רבי הזהב' (3:15.108-110) is read as 'the Rav Ravid ha-Zahav' (רביד הזהב): the printed רבי lacks the final ד of רביד, and the same book is named at 3:15.5-7; the printed Hebrew is kept in the token note.
The printed 'אלקבולי' (3:15.126) is transliterated as printed ('Alkaboli'); it may be a form of Alkabetz (אלקבץ). 'הר"מ' is read 'Rabbi Moshe' without a surname that fixes him.
The printed 'כ'' (3:15.119) in the list of names is left as the initial 'K.' (see the question).
Base text is Wikisource; a general line until the 1931 scan is collated (open question 2).
context: Beit Yosef is the commentary on the Tur; 'Maran' is the honorific the author gives its writer.
הלכה למשה מסיני: a law held to go back to Moses at Sinai; the author uses the phrase for a binding ruling.
